profile.name: Alex Ababu
profile.statement: I build software that people actually use.
profile.intro: Full-stack engineer focused on turning messy, real-world problems into fast, dependable products. I like the whole arc — from the first sketch to the thing shipping in production.
profile.availability: Open to Summer 2026 internships & new-grad roles

about.heading: Engineer first, translator always.
body: I'm a computer science student at Arizona State University who spends most of my free time shipping side projects. My favorite problems live at the seam between a clean system and a real person trying to get something done.
Whether I'm designing a data pipeline or a checkout flow, I try to keep two audiences in mind: the engineer who'll maintain it next year, and the person who just needs it to work today.

experience.summary: Built internal analytics tooling that cut a manual reporting process from two days to under an hour. Shipped three services to production and owned the on-call rotation for one of them.
Research on scheduling for distributed training jobs. Wrote the simulation harness the team now uses to benchmark new policies before touching real hardware.
First engineer on a two-person team. Took a campus-marketplace idea from a Figma file to 1,200 active students in a semester.

projects.title: Atlas
projects.summary: A course-planning platform that helps ASU students map four years of degree requirements in an afternoon instead of a semester.
projects.description: Atlas ingests the university catalog, models prerequisite chains as a directed graph, and lets students drag courses across semesters while it validates their plan in real time. The hard part wasn't the UI — it was reconciling a decade of inconsistent catalog data into something a solver could trust.
highlights: Constraint solver validates 4-year plans against prereqs and credit caps in under 50ms
Parsed 8,000+ catalog entries into a clean prerequisite graph
Grew to 4,300 students through word of mouth, zero marketing spend

projects.title: Signal
projects.summary: A tiny, self-hostable service that flags anomalies in time-series metrics before they page a human at 3am.
projects.description: Signal watches metric streams and learns each series' normal rhythm, then surfaces the handful of blips worth waking someone up for. It ships as a single Go binary with no external dependencies, so a small team can run it without standing up a whole observability stack.
highlights: Online detection with a rolling seasonal-decomposition model
Single 12MB binary — no database, no message queue required
Cut false-positive alerts by ~70% in a pilot deployment

projects.title: Tempo
projects.summary: A shared, real-time queue that keeps a room's music democratic — built in 36 hours and won Best UX.
projects.description: Everyone in the room adds songs from their phone; Tempo weighs votes and recency so no single person hijacks the speaker. Real-time sync runs over WebSockets with an optimistic UI, so the queue feels instant even on conference wifi.
highlights: Real-time queue sync across dozens of devices over WebSockets
Optimistic UI keeps interactions instant on flaky networks
Won Best UX out of 60 teams at SunHacks

projects.title: Forge
projects.summary: A CLI that scaffolds a fully-wired backend service — routes, tests, CI, and Docker — from a single config file.
projects.description: Forge grew out of my own frustration re-doing the same boilerplate for every side project. Point it at a short YAML spec and it generates a runnable service with linting, tests, and a deploy pipeline already green. It's the tool I now start every project with.
highlights: Generates a production-ready service from one YAML file
Pluggable templates so teams can encode their own conventions
Trimmed new-service setup from a day to about two minutes
